title: Caught Up to Paradise, Given a Thorn: Power in Weakness
summary: Continuing his reluctant boasting, Paul tells of a man in Christ caught up to the third heaven fourteen years earlier, but refuses to boast in it. To keep him from conceit he was given a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan; he pleaded three times for its removal, and the Lord answered that his grace is sufficient and his power is perfected in weakness. Paul then defends his conduct toward the Corinthians, announces a third visit, and voices his fear of finding quarreling and unrepented sin when he comes.
story: This chapter is the climax of the fool's speech that began in 11:16. Having boasted in his sufferings, Paul now turns to the kind of credential his rivals seem to have prized most: visions and revelations. He has one to tell, but he tells it in the third person and cuts it short, and he places beside it the thorn that keeps him humble. The Lord's answer to his prayer, "My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness", is the key to the whole letter. The rest of the chapter returns to the practical situation and prepares for the warnings of chapter 13.
historical:
"Fourteen years ago" (verse 2), counted back from a letter written around AD 55 or 56, places the vision in the early 40s. That falls in the years Paul spent in Syria and Cilicia after his conversion (Galatians 1:21), before Barnabas brought him to Antioch (Acts 11:25-26), a period about which very little is known. The vision is therefore not the Damascus road experience, which was earlier.

Paul's third visit (verse 14; 13:1) confirms that he had made a second, painful visit (2:1) not recorded in Acts. Acts 20:2-3 records that he spent three months in Greece, most likely based in Corinth, where he wrote Romans, so the visit he announces here seems to have taken place. The "signs, wonders, and miracles" of verse 12 are not described in the Acts account of Corinth, but Paul mentions them as something the Corinthians saw for themselves (compare Romans 15:18-19).
cultural:
Many Jewish writers of the period spoke of multiple heavens, often three or seven, and of visionaries being taken up through them. The "third heaven" and "Paradise" in verses 2-4 appear to refer to the same place, the presence of God. Paradise, a Persian loanword for an enclosed garden or park, was used in the Greek Old Testament for the garden of Eden and came to name the place of the righteous with God (Luke 23:43; Revelation 2:7). In a culture that honored those who had ecstatic experiences, a report of such a vision would be powerful currency. Paul's refusal to describe what he heard, and his telling of it in the third person, deliberately withholds that currency.

Verse 14 draws on the common assumption that parents save for their children, not the reverse. Paul presents himself as the Corinthians' father in the faith (1 Corinthians 4:15), who spends himself for them rather than living off them.
literary: Verses 1-10 are the heart of the fool's speech. The ascent is told with striking restraint: in the third person, with two repeated admissions of ignorance ("whether in the body or out of it I do not know, but God knows"), and with no content given. Then the story goes down instead of up: from paradise to a thorn, from revelations to weakness. Paul pleaded three times, and the Lord's reply is the only direct saying of the risen Christ quoted in the letter. Verse 10 condenses the paradox into a single line: "when I am weak, then I am strong." Verses 11-13 end the fool's speech with irony ("Forgive me this wrong!"), and verses 14-21 turn to his coming visit, with a list of vices in verses 20-21 that shows what Paul fears finding.

outline.t: A man caught up to the third heaven
The thorn in the flesh: power perfected in weakness
The end of the fool's speech: signs of an apostle
A parent who seeks not your possessions but you

doctrines.note: Paul's prayer for relief was answered with a no, and with a promise. The chapter does not teach that God always removes suffering in answer to faith; it teaches that God's grace is sufficient within it and that his power is displayed through weakness. This has been a lasting comfort to Christians living with chronic illness, disability, or unrelieved hardship.

Paul "pleaded with the Lord" three times, honestly and repeatedly, for relief. His prayer was heard, but the answer was not the one he asked for. Prayer here is not a technique for getting what we want but a relationship in which the Lord speaks and gives what is needed.

The thorn is described as both "given" (by implication, by God, to keep Paul from conceit) and "a messenger of Satan". The chapter holds together God's overruling purpose and Satan's hostile intent, as the book of Job does, without resolving how they relate.

words.note: Skolops, a sharp stake, a thorn or splinter. In the Greek Old Testament it appears in Numbers 33:55, where the Canaanites left in the land will be thorns in Israel's sides. Whether Paul means a small painful splinter or something larger, the word conveys a persistent, piercing pain.

Arkeo, to be enough, to suffice. The Lord's reply is "My grace is sufficient for you". The present tense in the Greek suggests ongoing sufficiency: grace that is enough now and continues to be enough, not a one-time supply.

Astheneia, weakness, which can mean illness, frailty, or lack of status and power. It is the key word of chapters 11-13. Paul does not boast in weakness as such, but in weakness as the place where Christ's power rests on him.

Paradeisos, paradise, a Persian loanword for a walled garden. In the Greek Old Testament it names the garden of Eden; in Jewish and Christian use it came to mean the dwelling of God with the righteous. Jesus promised it to the thief on the cross (Luke 23:43).

christ: The Lord who speaks in verse 9 is the risen Christ, and his words, "My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness", are a summary of the gospel itself. Christ's own power was displayed through the ultimate weakness of the cross, as 13:4 will say. Paul wants "the power of Christ" to rest on him (verse 9), a phrase some interpreters connect with the Old Testament picture of God's presence dwelling in the tabernacle. Everything in Paul's life that looks like failure becomes a place where Christ's strength is seen. The pattern of the chapter, ascent refused and weakness embraced, is the pattern of Christ, who did not grasp at glory but humbled himself.

hard.q: What was Paul's thorn in the flesh, and why didn't God remove it?
hard.a:
No one knows, and Paul does not say. Over the centuries readers have made three main kinds of suggestion. Many think it was a physical ailment, since "flesh" often means the body and Galatians 4:13-15 mentions an illness that tested the Galatians and hints that Paul's eyes were affected; proposals have included eye disease, recurring fever such as malaria, migraines, epilepsy, or a speech difficulty. Others think it was persecution or opposition, especially the false apostles of chapter 11, since the phrase recalls Numbers 33:55, where enemies are thorns in Israel's sides, and since "messenger of Satan" can describe a person. A third line of interpretation, common in medieval times, took it as a spiritual temptation or inner struggle. Each view has supporters, and the text does not allow a firm decision. Its vagueness has let readers with many kinds of suffering see themselves in it.

Why it was not removed, Paul does explain: it kept him from becoming conceited, and it became the place where Christ's power rested on him. That is not a universal rule that God never heals, since the New Testament records many healings. It is an honest testimony that God sometimes answers prayer for relief with grace to endure, and that such an answer is not a sign of his absence.

questions: Paul had a remarkable spiritual experience but chose not to build his authority on it. Why might God value weakness more than spectacular experience in his servants?
Have you prayed repeatedly for something to be taken away and received a different answer? How does "My grace is sufficient for you" speak to that experience?
Paul says he seeks not the Corinthians' possessions but them. What would it look like to love people in your care in that way?
